en: Applying sunscreen with SPF 30 blocks about 97 percent of the sun's harmful UVB rays to prevent sunburns.
Wading in floodwaters after a typhoon can expose you to leptospirosis, a serious bacterial infection spread through rat urine.
Boiling tap water for at least one minute kills harmful bacteria and viruses, making it safe to drink during outages.
Wearing gloves while gardening prevents cuts and protects your skin from soilborne bacteria like tetanus that enter through open wounds.
Wearing an N95 mask during a volcanic eruption filters out fine volcanic ash particles that can severely damage your lungs.
Looking directly at a solar eclipse without certified solar filters can cause permanent eye damage because intense rays burn the retina.
During a full moon, stronger gravitational pull creates higher spring tides, which can cause unexpected and dangerous sneaker waves on beaches.
Dropping to the ground and covering your head under a sturdy table protects you from falling debris during an earthquake.
If you hear thunder, you are close enough to be struck by lightning, so you must immediately seek shelter indoors.
Warmer temperatures from climate change speed up the breeding cycle of Aedes mosquitoes, increasing the risk of dengue fever in your community.
High humidity prevents your sweat from evaporating quickly, making the heat index feel much hotter than the actual air temperature.
Finding the North Star, or Polaris, helps you determine true north and avoid getting lost if you are hiking without a compass.
